paragraphs.text: IV. THE LIFE OF THE BLESSED MONK ANTONY. PREFACE.

As fighters rise to the sound of trumpets, and as horses are spurred by the iron heel to a faster pace, so the virtue of those who went before us stirs us and gives strength to young talents. Whoever rereads the time-honoured exercises and deeds of the ancients is fired toward the fruit of good discipline, with the prize of praise set before him. The image of past glory is held fast by a chain of tongues so that it may reach later generations. Nothing that reading, the friend of serene deeds, has taken up may perish over the ages. So the long life of eloquence overcomes the narrow limits of mortal nature without the danger of a fight, and through it the way of life of the best men knows no setting, even when they themselves fall. The body, it is true, is returned to its origin, and the spirit, appointed from above, goes back to its own Author. Yet for those whose uprightness has been committed to books, death itself is full of life. A sterner interpreter might say: a mind that has finished with the world renounces the sweetness of praise; once freed from the bonds of the flesh, it has no wish for the things it did amid the uncertainties of the world to be known. Rather, the prison of the body handed such men back to their Maker with no loss of freedom, while the soul, walking among defiled things but intent on our God, doubled its brightness and, keeping to the lines of the heavenly commandments, never felt the seductive error of this present light. But for us let these things come to life again, and for our profit let them be preserved. If we lack the zeal to pursue better things, that zeal must come from the example of those who carry before us the torch of their own way of life. And you, venerable Abbot Leontius, who laid this work upon me, help me with your prayer as I falter, and enrich the dryness of my pen with the rain of your holy prayers. For you will make outstanding in merit, as I trust, what you yourself ordered me to undertake. It is easy for your blessedness to fill out a meagre eloquence with the rich dishes of innocence. Believe me, the fault or the genius of a style wrung out of me will reflect on you; and unless you strengthen its substance with your religious authority, the faith of your judgement will seem to have limped, and to have chosen someone less fit when you entrusted to him the charge of this venerable labour.

Therefore, as I am about to tell of the distinctions of blessed Antony, I must first call upon the majesty of the Holy Spirit. May he who made Antony rich in deeds govern me with the reins of the tongue as I set them out, and may he soon wash away the filth of my lips with the fire of the prophet's coal. Otherwise the clouds of my conscience may leave the light of Antony's life poor where it deserves the fullest praise, or my withered want of speech may rob it of its beauty. Blessed be the undivided Trinity, our God, who bade his servant Antony, raised so high by the dowry of so many virtues, to enter the gate of this light near the banks of the river Danube, in the city of Valeria, with Secundinus as his father. Although he drew a radiant sense of himself from the splendour of his birth, he outshone the brilliance of his distinguished stock with the rays of his character. He surpassed the beauty of his blood by the brightness of his mind and rose above the gleaming lamp of his lineage by the serenity of his deeds. So he became victor over the very pedigree by which, at his birth, he had surpassed everyone. While he was still hanging at his mother's breasts, the grace of God did not abandon the one it foreknew, and the heavenly dispensation did not allow him to be without favour, since it had approved him as one full of the endeavours that would earn reward. So that he would not break the commitments of his holy purpose through the coaxing of his parents, he was deprived of his father's guardianship at about eight years of age. Soon, however, at an age that knows nothing of pretence, he flew to that most illustrious man Severinus. As Severinus caressed him with kisses, he read the good things to come in the boy as though they were already accomplished, for he was a man from whose merits nothing was hidden. Everywhere he proclaimed with pious voice that this boy would be his partner. I believe he did so in order that the hope so announced might strengthen the beginner in his apprenticeship.

But after that blessed man was taken from human affairs, Antony joined the service of Bishop Constantius, who was then at the height of his renown, and dedicated the first beginnings of his life to glorious works. The bishop had him begin his heavenly service among the notaries of the church, for that venerable priest was our Antony's paternal uncle. Yet he never softened the rigour of his teaching for the sake of kinship, nor did he let his pupil grow so secure in their relationship as to stop fearing him. He showed him a teacher's favour only by way of strictness. His care for his follower was measured exactly by his judgements of him, and Antony read his own merit in his teacher's face. But now the full measure of sins was threatening Pannonia with destruction. The root of its strength had already been cut, and the condition of that region had sunk into decline. Through the raids of various peoples, the daily crop of swords had mown down the harvest of the nobility, and wrath laid waste, plundering lands that had been fertile in human offspring. Franks, Heruli and Saxons were by now carrying out manifold kinds of cruelty like wild beasts. These diverse nations, enslaved to superstitious cults, believed that their gods were soothed by human slaughter, and that their deities were never favourable unless they had appeased them with the blood of their own fellows. They trusted that the anger of the heavenly ones would cease if innocent blood were shed, and to return into favour with their gods they used to offer up the deaths of their own kin. Above all, whomever the title of a religious office marked out they sacrificed as more pleasing victims, thinking that the indignation of the godhead was ended by the throats of the pious, and that the occasion of offence was turned into the matter of grace. Amid these storms of the times, while the land was being allotted to foreign guests, Bishop Constantius was released by the common law of humankind, so that he might have nothing in the world to lean on.

After his death, with Christ as guide, servants brought our Antony to the regions of Italy to which heaven had assigned him. First he crossed the threshold of the Valtellina, the valley that has received that name. Nature's loveliness, building it with the arms of mountains on either side, makes it rich, and from its fertile peaks endows the rich soil with a multitude of streams. That soil answers its greedy farmers as fully as their boundless desires could wish. Yet it is not so heavy with grain, so dowered with pastures, so planted with orchards or so glad with rivers that the grace of the newcomer did not give it more than the varied and distinctive beauty of its own nature. There he joined the priest Marius, who had mastery over unclean spirits. For such is the way of things: the companions a newcomer finds make his character known, and one who is unknown by origin becomes famous through his affection for those like him. The secret mind is detected through its companions, and whoever cannot clearly judge a newcomer's conscience is allowed to judge the stranger by his friends. When blessed Marius looked at him with those eyes by which minds are seen, and with hidden gaze examined the beauty of the inner man, he wished to join him to the body of the clergy and to dedicate so outstanding a person to the ranks of the church. But Antony fled that honour like a cup of poison. He had always held power to be a lowly thing, and he preferred patient service to royal dominion.

So that he would not mingle too long in the allurements of human society and drink in its contagion, he chose a retreat not far from the tomb of the blessed martyr Fidelis. There Lake Como lays down its menace, worthy of the Ionian sea, when the reins of the land hold it back with banks set against it, so that it may stray no farther. In that place a mountain gleams, its summit thrust into the clouds, so high that it outstrips the sight. But it is as hard to climb as it is proud in its size. Before our monk it had been open to no one's steps, and the fear it inspired had kept any human foot off its sheer rocks. For a long time, with no one to frighten them, its sheer crags had given safe lairs to wild beasts, and it was the kinder to the beasts the more terribly it threatened the forays of farmers. On this mountain the servant of God chose his home, and the only reason it pleased him was that it in no way flattered the eye. Of the world's benefits he took nothing with him but a little pulse and a mattock to work the earth, and he consecrated a path that no one had known because the ground was so rough. When Antony came to grips with those ridges, they lost their untamed law of nature: once he had entered, the ways were unlocked and lay open to all who wished to come. There, however, he found two old men whom long dwelling had so mingled with the dens of beasts that rumour told the world nothing of them. I think I have said all there is to say about their life and holiness when I have plainly made known the dwelling they sought out of fear of God. Shortly afterwards one of them was taken up; he laid down the bulk of his earthly prison, and his happy soul took up heavenly health again. For at the time of his release a pillar of fire, reaching all the way to heaven, was presented to blessed Antony's eyes. I believe this was so that the faith of that venerable man, and the ardour that burns away vices, might be shown forth in a symbolic fire, at a time when the worshipper of God there was spreading all the sails of his strength to the heavenly disciplines and catching in the folds of soul and body the winds that drive out the chaff. I would rightly recount his vigils, his fasts and his constant reading, if I did not have things more worthy of mention. He never took food unless his poor body was failing, and never relaxed his care with rest until the duty of his office was done. But why should I go over the instruments of perfection that this perfect man possessed, or the steps by which he climbed to the heights, when it has been plainly shown that he holds the heights? He knew how to follow the outlines of the disciplines through various labours without ever growing arrogant from his labour; and though everything he did was worthy of praise, he believed that to be praised was a loss to virtue. Everything in his deeds shone with the light of good repute, yet nothing was put on for show. The severity of his mind stood out in his body, and his unpainted face portrayed the anger his soul had taken up against faults. You could see his eyes stern against the world's wickedness, and the soldier of Christ waging tireless wars against the blandishments of the world. When did that countenance ever relax its bearing into laughter, or let the weakness of mirth break the rigour of its proper order?

Meanwhile, as he was fulfilling the office of a monk in everything, as though bound by a seal, a certain man came to him. Love for his betrothed had driven him to crime, and passion and indignation had provoked him to shed human blood. He believed he could escape his conscience by changing lands, and find in other parts of the province the innocence he had lost under the leadership of fury. So, veiled in simplicity, he carried a murderer into the secret places of the wilderness, thinking that those set in God's service could see nothing of his deeds but his outward appearance. He feigned humility with an artful look, and, composing himself in a submission fabricated by the devices of a deceitful plan, he covered the filth of his crimes with careful screens. It is hard for anyone but God to detect what is wrapped in the outward show of obedience. Abasement shrewdly hides a crime, and crimes seldom burst into the light when their author has known how to bury them under the paint of compliance. At once, however, that accustomed informer was present and unlocked the secrets of the hidden conscience with the key of the divine voice. It addressed Antony in these words, teaching him to recognise more than a man can, and unmasking the one who covered a robber with a coarse garment: 'Beware,' it said, 'of mingling a man guilty of so great a crime with your holy community. Do not be a careless judge and join a wolf to the sheep or a viper to the lambs. This man drove out a soul granted by the hands of God through the fragments of a crushed throat. In murderous fury he seized his brother and, binding his throat, loosed his life from its dwelling. Due destruction pursues him, and he who did not spare human blood will not escape the yoke of punishment. Let mercy give way; toward criminals strictness must be kept. So put an end to slumber and drive out this enemy of the heavenly commandments, so that the bright way of life of those who live with you may not be violated by the dark contagion of this newcomer.' At once Antony obeyed the divine commands. He summoned the man, convicted him of lying, and with [?] mouth went through all the deeds of that guilty conscience. Caught out, the man was terrified to see a human being recount crimes he had committed with no human witness. He asked for provisions for the road and, trembling, prepared to flee. But vengeance, following at his heels, seized the guilty man at once, and his death proclaimed his crime atoned for. Thus the word of the just man could not be without power.

Meanwhile the holy man became known throughout the neighbouring regions through the tongues of treacherous fame. So that it would not breed boastfulness out of celebrity, remedies were provided before the disease could grow. For what old or feeble man, with eagerness as his guide, did not cross the precipices of that road? When desire gave them health, how could sickness keep hold of their bodies? Alarmed by these crowds, blessed Antony believed he must flee to more secret parts of the wilderness, so that the devotion of individuals would not become the mother of hateful arrogance, and so that the ruin of his stricter purpose would not arise from the many forms of favour. Soon he chose a retreat, commended to him by an overhanging rock, and there for many years he lived alone, truly a monk, without a single human companion. The mountain solitude gave him wild beasts for comrades. The bellowing of the bear and the menacing growls of other beasts took the place of pleasant conversation. At that time a rather wanton bear, which was to bring him more glory, got in among his cabbages. They were flourishing with full-grown leaves and seemed to exult with a kind of cheerfulness for their master, but the bear trampled them savagely and laid them waste, so that no hope at all remained of that simple crop. Antony beat it with his staff, sternly ordered it to depart, and soon compelled it to go off to the other beasts as a witness of his power and a messenger of what it had suffered. So the faithful promise of the Lord was fulfilled, which promised his followers that all venom and all beasts would obey them. Again, as he was walking along his chosen path, a beast came roaring at him. By a command alone he alarmed it and made it open the way and abandon the road it had blocked.

But see, once again on swift wings, true to its habit of betrayal, rumour made known where the servant of God was living, and different people held different opinions about him. Then it became plain from the many visitors that nothing stands in the way of those who desire: heights are levelled, chasms bridged, overhangs not feared. But against greater snares he set his hand to a stronger plan, so that the enemy would not steal in through arrogance, and so that in his old age he would not lose what by virtue he had kept safe in his apprenticeship. For the devil's contest is fiercer against the strong, and he attacks with greater forces those who have experienced his assaults and subdued them with the sweat of their strength. Turning everything over within himself, he strengthened his mind with a brief address: 'What are we doing, my mind, still weighed down by the load of the world's burden, not yet spewed out by the prison of the body to your Author? You can have no sure confidence of perfection while you are still shut up in the frailty of the flesh. The things that seem safest are full of dangers. You understand the seductions of your enemy when you are praised by the voice of everyone. See what snares you labour under: whatever place we go to cannot stay hidden, and the enemy's persecution reveals our hiding place. Let us seek out the army of the saints, and with a burning longing go in search of that cohort on the island of Lérins. The adversary, who until now has assailed a man on his own, will fear him once he is set among a multitude hostile to the enemy. That battle line, drawn up for combat, is always on watch, and drives off the attacker pierced with many blows. They count as many triumphs as the wars the devil has waged on them. They do not fear whenever the shrill trumpet has announced that Satan is near; rather, the fighting sharpens them. Daily combat has always made them skilled and strong, just as a longer peace makes men slack.'

With these words he left his cell to the brothers whom love for him had gathered there, and appeared unexpectedly at Lérins. His face, adorned with the pallor of fasting, proclaimed a man of outstanding merits. While his most splendid leanness revealed the brightness of the hidden man within, his accustomed herald was not lacking either: report described the spotless beauty of his way of life in abundant words and a rich account. Mingling with the elders and the most eminent, he saw that the lamp of their deeds blazed with no lesser fire, and he measured the light of his own flame when he saw another's. It was as when, among the ornaments of heaven and the stars glittering in full brilliance, the brightness of a newly arriving star is joined to them. They vie without envy to double their rays, and by increasing their light they surpass the beauty of the newcomer. One star commends its face with longer tresses, another with purer ones; a stronger flame enriches one, a clearer one ennobles another through the spaces of the night. So the discipline that comes from Christ accompanied our Antony through all his changes of place. Yet he took care that on that island, the nurse of saints, though he excelled in merit, he should not seem to be preferred to anyone in honour, for he knew that what is planted in the root of humility rises to bear fruit a hundredfold. Gentle with the young, grave with the mature, learned with the learned, humble in his bearing toward the simple, he gathered through his affection that whole legion of the Lord's flock, different in conduct and drawn from many nations, as though into one soul. There, for two years, he surpassed even himself. Then he laid down the burden of this world and, victorious over the snares the cunning of the ancient serpent lays, exchanged our day and the light of this present age for the gaining of everlasting light. I pass over how the brightness of his death set its seal on his life, so that by setting everything out I may not seem to have lingered over his praises rather than told the truth. It is as when someone finds a grove thick with dense foliage and cuts a garland from it with a blade: because he takes only a little, he does not take away the spirit of the wood. In the same way I have left the deeds of our Antony that my pen has not touched for better writers to tell. I may perhaps be outdone in the river of eloquence, but no one will surpass me in affection for him. Let whoever comes after me boast of a harvest of skill. No one will snatch from me the favour of the blessed man, for I was the first to undertake the telling of his good deeds.
